extracted.intended_audience: practitioners/respondents and counsel in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria for filing and evaluating a request for reconsideration of a USPTO Director’s final disciplinary decision under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c), and related rules on waiver, stays, admissibility, and timeliness in OED proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/regulatory standard for reconsideration (37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: "No request for reconsideration or modification shall be granted unless the request is based on newly discovered evidence or error of law or fact, and the requestor must demonstrate that any newly discovered evidence could not have been discovered any earlier by due diligence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests must be grounded in one of the listed bases (new evidence or error of law or fact). Mere disagreement with the final decision is not a basis. Newly discovered evidence must also meet the due-diligence/unavailability requirement. The standard is narrow and strictly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous use of Federal Rules 59(e) and 60 as guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO may look to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 59(e) and 60 for guidance because those rules are most similar to § 11.56(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal caselaw applying Rules 59(e)/60 has been used as persuasive authority to construe § 11.56(c). The Director’s practice of consulting those rules is long-standing and not inconsistent with § 11.56(c). However, referencing them is guidance only — not a substitution for the regulation’s text.

rubrics_metrics.name: New evidence must have been unavailable earlier (due diligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new evidence submitted must not have been available before the issuance of the final decision; the requester must demonstrate it could not have been discovered earlier by due diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence available prior to the final decision is not a basis for reconsideration (see Boryan v. United States and related authority). The requester must explain why the evidence could not have been found earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration is not a vehicle to relitigate or rehash prior arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for reconsideration are not a vehicle to state a party’s disagreement with a final judgment or to relitigate issues previously decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments or evidence that were or could have been presented on appeal cannot be presented anew on reconsideration. Case law cautions that mere disagreement or rehashing prior submissions does not justify relief (e.g., Hutchinson, Arthur, Wadley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary-remedy doctrine (sparingly granted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for reconsideration are extraordinary remedies reserved only for extraordinary circumstances and are seldom granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat motions to alter or amend judgments narrowly; the USPTO follows this approach. Requesters must show compelling, exceptional circumstances to succeed (citing Dowell, Projects Mgmt. Co., Netscape).

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of issues not raised on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments not raised or developed during the appeal are waived on reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an appellant did not raise an issue in their appeal or reply brief to the Director, they generally cannot raise it in a § 11.56(c) request (see In re Correll, In re Walpert). Examples in the order: delay/timeliness and certain constitutional/equal protection claims were waived because not presented on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness/delay and applicability of 37 C.F.R. § 11.39(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.39(d) permits an ALJ to issue an initial decision more than nine months after a complaint if circumstances preclude issuance within nine months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that the Director delayed improperly must be raised timely; transmittal delay may be distinguished from issuance. A delay argument is waived if not raised earlier and will fail if the regulation permits the delay and the ALJ documented circumstances (e.g., pandemic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application and notice of § 11.5 definition of 'practice before the Office'
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges to the breadth or vagueness of the § 11.5 definition must be timely raised and, when the ALJ relies on conduct explicitly listed in § 11.5, such challenges lack merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the ALJ grounds misconduct on specific conduct enumerated in § 11.5 (e.g., advising clients on matters before the Office), a void-for-vagueness challenge is unlikely to succeed. Failure to develop the argument on appeal results in waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of hearsay and cross-examination rights in OED proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO permits the introduction of hearsay evidence in disciplinary proceedings; an assertion that hearsay was improperly admitted or that the requester was denied cross-examination is insufficient without showing an error of law or fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing the Final Order and relevant authority, mere restatement of a hearsay objection is inadequate. Parties are expected to call witnesses and pursue cross-examination at the hearing; failure to subpoena or call witnesses is a party decision and not necessarily reversible error. Arguments invoking APA § 556(d) are waived if not raised previously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for stays of discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.57(c)) — exceptional circumstances required
rubrics_metrics.description: "Except as provided for in § 11.56(c), an order for discipline in a final decision will not be stayed except on proof of exceptional circumstances."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stay of discipline is not governed by the federal TRO/preliminary injunction standard; petitioners must prove exceptional circumstances. Generalized claims of reputational or financial injury are insufficient; allowing continued practice during court review can harm the public and the USPTO. Failure to show exceptional circumstances requires denial of a stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to show likelihood of success and irreparable harm is fact-dependent and constrained by regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments borrowed from federal injunctive-relief standards (likelihood of success, irreparable harm) do not substitute for the § 11.57(c) exceptional-circumstances requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While federal injunctive standards may be referenced, they are not controlling where the regulation imposes an 'exceptional circumstances' threshold; reliance on those standards without showing exceptional circumstances is insufficient to obtain a stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural posture and notice considerations (prior participation defeats 'no notice' claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who has previously participated in or been counsel in other reconsideration matters may be on notice of USPTO practices (e.g., consulting Rules 59(e)/60), and thus cannot credibly claim lack of notice regarding those practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior involvement in similar proceedings or representation in cases where USPTO used the federal-rule analogy undermines arguments that practitioners lacked notice of the Director’s interpretive approach.
